newsitem.title: GERMANY: German-French plan for more EU flexibility.
newsitem.headline: German-French plan for more EU flexibility.

text.p: Germany and France said on Friday that as many European Union members as possible should join the accelerated integration schemes the EU plans to start after finishing its current Maastricht treaty review talks.

Foreign ministers Klaus Kinkel and Herve de Charette said in a discussion paper that some states that wanted to push ahead, for example by creating a single European currency, should not be held up by those unable or unwilling to join.
But, in forging ahead, member states should keep "the goal of the highest possible number of participants", they said.
"No member state can have a veto. No member state willing and able to participate can be excluded," they said.

Germany originally came in for heavy criticism in 1994 when leading Christian Democrats proposed a "hard core Europe" that would create an economic and monetary union (EMU) consisting only of Germany, France and the Benelux countries.

But officials from Germany and France, the two main champions of further EU integration, have since stressed that the new "flexibility clause" would not turn Europe into a collection of closed shops as critics charged.
A foreign ministry statement issued with the discussion paper said simply: "We do not want a hard core Europe!"
Germany and France plan to submit the paper to the EU's inter-governmental conference at its next meeting on Monday.
Kinkel and de Charette said EU members could choose to forge ahead with their own smaller-scale integration in foreign and defence policy as well as in legal affairs.
Only a qualified majority would be needed to start such initiatives, but the states participating in a more coordinated policy would take their decisions unanimously.
These plans must respect the current integration level achieved by the EU, the discussion paper stressed.

"The introduction of such a clause should enable the deepening of European integration to be continued," the paper said. "It can can only be directed forwards, even if only some of the member states are ready to progress at first."
